title: Chapter 26: The Black Mask
paragraphs: Agdash woke as if it had not slept at all, only pretended.

First the city wheezed. Somewhere deep in the lower tiers the bellows stirred, and their heavy breathing crawled through the stone streets in thick waves of hot air. Then the chains began to ring. Then the hammers joined in: one, then another, then a third, dozens and hundreds of blows scattered through workshops, mine yards, forges, and cellar foundries. Only after that came the voices. Sharp, tired, angry, alive.

The city of the fire elves did not greet morning with birdsong. Birds had stopped loving this world long ago. Morning here opened with the scrape of metal, the stink of soot, the curses of merchants, and the shrieks of thin children running between basalt supports as if they had been born in the cracks between stones.
Anar walked through the courtyards of the lower residential tier and watched his own feet.
He did not like this city.

It was not exactly a final opinion. More of a working version. Agdash was too large, too hot, too loud, too certain of its right to crush anyone who had not found a place within it. It stood on black basalt, overgrown with bridges, terraces, pipes, lava channels, and other people's lives. It smelled of spices, rust, sour sweat, coal, cheap oil, and something else - an old fear worked deeper into the walls than soot.

After fifteen days in a cell, Anar had learned to hear smells more clearly. He did not like that either. A man learns unpleasant things about himself when he is locked in a stone box with a drunken orc. For instance, that he can get used to almost anything. Even the stink. Even humiliation. Even the way a guard beyond the bars looks at him like trash that has not yet been carried out only because the shift is not over.
He pushed his hands deeper into the pockets of his re-stitched jacket and kept walking.

The courtyards of Agdash were arranged strangely. From the street they looked like ordinary gaps between buildings, but if you turned beneath a low arch, an entire inner world opened up: stone stairways, laundry drying over pipes, water barrels, tiny stalls under awnings, children, old people, women with faces dried by exhaustion, and thin fire elves warming themselves beside braziers though the air around them was already hot. In one courtyard an old man repaired leather straps and hummed softly in a language Anar did not know. In another, two little girls played with smooth bone stones arranged in a circle on the dust. In a third, a skinny boy with a bandaged shoulder was teaching his younger brother how to hold a wooden sword.
Anar stopped for a moment and watched.
The boy was ten, maybe twelve. Age was hard to judge in this world. Even children here looked as if they had already buried someone important.
The older boy demonstrated an overhead strike.
The younger copied him. Awkwardly, too wide, opening his stomach.
The older one immediately jabbed him in the side with the stick.
The boy yelped, took offense, but did not cry.
Anar turned away.

He suddenly felt disgusted by his own idleness. Not merely bored, not merely empty - disgusted. Zhenya worked. Yura worked. Alexander sat in the palace, where every word could cost someone a ration, a weapon, or a head. Ravan fought on the training grounds as if he meant to punch a road back home out of the world. Even Stephanie, a fire elf girl with a pathetic spark instead of flame, went beyond the walls and burned her own fingers because she wanted to become stronger.
Anar, meanwhile, walked.
Walked again.
As if, if he passed through enough courtyards, someone would carry the meaning of life out to him on a little sign.
He gave a short, bitter smile at himself.

A crowd of workers had gathered near a stall selling smoked roots. Behind the counter, a broad-shouldered elf woman turned thick dark tubers over an iron grate, coating them in a sharp red sauce. The smell was so strong it stung Anar's eyes. He thought that eating would be nice, remembered how much money he had left after the room at the Red Cauldron, and decided that spiritual development was more important than breakfast.
A few steps later, he saw the notice wall.

In truth, it was not a wall but a massive slab of pale stone set into the black basalt at the meeting point of three alleys. Notices hung on it in several layers: coarse paper, strips of leather, wooden tablets, scraps of cloth marked with burned symbols. They overlapped one another like scales on a sick fish. Somewhere, someone was searching for a missing miner. Somewhere, someone offered two measures of dried beans for an intact boot sole. Somewhere, a city magistrate reminded citizens that leaving the walls without a mark was punishable by a fine, and a repeat offense by prison.
Anar grimaced.
The word "prison" had been getting into his eyes too often lately.
But his gaze did not catch on that.

At the center of the slab, over the older orders, hung a fresh sheet. Four bronze nails pinned it in place, and its edges had not yet gathered dust. The ink was dark red, thick, almost obscenely festive. The first line was written in large, severe letters.
OPEN TOURNAMENT OF THE RING OF AGDASH.
Below, in smaller script:

In seven days, free-entry bouts will be held at the Great Arena. Participation is permitted to anyone who possesses hands, feet, a name of their own, and the readiness to die beneath it. Registration at the western guard table of the arena until sunset of the fifth day. To the victor - gold, the right of weapon choice, and a place on the list of special city fighters for hire.
Anar read it once.
Then a second time.
Then a third, because some of the words sounded too tempting and too stupid at the same time.

He understood "the right of weapon choice" only vaguely. He understood "gold" immediately. He understood "a place on the list of city fighters" well enough. But "anyone who possesses hands, feet, a name of their own, and the readiness to die beneath it" pleased him.
There was something honest in that phrase.

Agdash lied often. It lied with the grandeur of its palace. It lied with beautiful arches behind which cellars rotted. It lied with words about duty when it sent boys to the walls. But here it did not lie. Do you want the arena? Come. Will you die? It happens. At least it will be under your own name.
Anar raised a hand and ran his fingers along the bottom line. The paper was dense, rough against his skin.
Tournament.
Arena.

He imagined a ring of sand, stone stands, the roar of a crowd. He imagined himself standing in the center while the air discharged around him, blue electricity crawling over his fingers, and someone finally stopped looking at him like a useless stranger.
For one second, the image was pleasant.
Then he imagined some local mountain of muscle breaking his neck in the first round.
That image was convincing too.
Anar took his hand away from the notice.
Behind him, someone coughed. Two workers smeared with coal dust were looking at him and grinning. One was missing his left ear; the other had a burn scar across his entire neck.
"The stranger's heading for the Ring," said the earless one.
The second snorted.
"Let him. The sand needs fertilizing too."
Anar slowly turned his head.

The workers immediately pretended the notice was very interesting. People in this world were brave when they spoke to someone's back. When they had to meet the eyes, bravery often turned into ordinary business.

Anar could have answered. He very much wanted to. He had already come up with three versions: one rude, one very rude, and one involving the family history of the earless worker. But then he remembered fifteen days with Gryz, the filthy porridge, the bars, and the sharp-cheeked guard who had calmly told him that Avotu held no power here.
He inhaled.
Exhaled.
And went to find the western guard table of the arena.
That turned out to be harder than it sounded.

Agdash did not like straight roads. It was a city built by beings who clearly believed that stairs should not lead somewhere, but test character. The street climbed, broke, ducked beneath a gallery, emerged onto a narrow bridge over a glowing channel, then dropped down again, where pipes hung overhead and some sort of hides dried between them. Anar asked for directions three times. The first elf pretended not to understand his language. The second asked for a coin. The third, an old woman with a basket of ash bread, silently pointed one long finger toward the arches and said:
"Follow the noise. The arena is always noisy, even when it is silent."
She was right.
He heard it before he saw it.

Not the roar of a crowd - there was no tournament yet. But the stone around the arena seemed to hold the memory of shouting. The squares near it sounded different. Footsteps echoed harder here, voices dropped lower, merchants called louder. By the walls they sold training wraps, cheap knives, dried meat, bruise salves, amulets of doubtful use, and little clay figurines of fighters with broken-off arms.

The Great Arena of Agdash stood on the boundary between the residential and military tiers. From the outside it resembled not entertainment but an ancient wound lined with stone to keep it from bleeding out. Black arcs of arches rose high above, pitted and marked by old fire. Between the columns hung faded banners: red, brown, gray, bearing the symbols of houses, guilds, and companies, many of which probably no longer existed. Above the main entrance, words had been carved in old elven. Anar could not read them, but for some reason he was certain the meaning was simple: enter alive, leave however you can.
The western guard table stood beneath a side arch.

There was an awning of darkened leather. Under it sat two scribes, one thin and young, the other old, with a face like stone. Nearby, leaning against a column, a guard in leather-and-metal armor was being bored. A short blade hung at his hip, and a dulled mark of the city watch sat on his chest. The guard had a broad, reddish face and small merry eyes, the eyes of a man who enjoyed other people's mistakes.

Three hopefuls stood before the table. The first was a huge fire elf with arms like beams. The second was a woman with one shaved temple and a pair of thin blades across her back. The third was a short, stocky half-orc who kept rolling his neck as though he was about to butt heads with the gate.
Anar took his place at the end of the line.
He did not like waiting. But after prison, a line in the open air felt almost like a gift from fate.

The big one registered quickly. The woman gave her name so quietly Anar did not hear it, then pressed her thumb to the sheet. The half-orc argued at length about whether he could compete with a chain hammer if the hammer belonged to his cousin and the cousin was still alive but very far away. The scribe said the city accepted no responsibility for family disputes concerning weapons. The half-orc was satisfied.
At last Anar stepped forward.
He nodded to the scribe.
"Hello. I want to register for the tournament."
The young scribe raised his eyes. The old one did not even move. But the guard by the column brightened at once, like a dog catching the scent of a funny death.
"You?" he asked.
Anar turned to him.
"Me."

The guard pushed away from the column and came closer. He measured Anar from head to toe: narrow face, foreign jacket, scrape on one cheekbone, careless posture, no sword, no armor, no properly respectful fear.
"Hear that, Laren?" he said to the young scribe, not hiding his smile. "The boy wants the Ring."
Laren the scribe coughed into his fist. The old scribe continued writing as if the conversation did not exist.
"What's wrong with that?" Anar asked.
"Nothing," said the guard. "I like brave men. Especially when they don't have time to suffer long."
Someone nearby laughed.

Anar felt the familiar warmth rising inside him. Not kind warmth. Not comforting warmth. The kind that made his fingers want to curl on their own, while the air around his nails began to smell of storm.
"I need registration," he said evenly. "Not a lecture."

"A lecture is exactly what you need, stranger. Free of charge. Have you looked at yourself? On the arena, the first hit will fold you in half. Not even in a pretty way. Just clap - and done. Then the cleaners will argue over where to put you: with the people or with nature's mistakes."
The laughter grew louder.
Anar looked at the scribe.
"Register me."
The young scribe hesitated. He had already taken up his pen, but the guard placed his palm on the edge of the table.
"Wait, Laren. We are not beasts. We should save the man's life."
"I'm actually strong," Anar said.
The guard blinked, then smiled broadly.
"Of course."
"Avotu himself acknowledged me."

This time the laughter broke off strangely. Not because everyone was impressed. More because the name dropped into the square like a coin into mud: it rang, but no one knew whether it was worth bending down for.
The guard narrowed his eyes.
"Who?"
"Avotu," Anar repeated.
"And who's that? Some new tavern singer?"
Anar slowly turned his whole body toward him.

"Have you been living under a rock? Avotu is one of the twelve students of Sivarus. A legendary warrior. Fire elf. Black flame. A sword that could cut off half your self-respect, if anyone could find the other half."
The corner of the young scribe's mouth twitched. The old scribe finally lifted his eyes.
The guard was no longer smiling broadly. Now his smile was thin.
"Ah," he drawled. "So you're that one."

Anar understood that things were about to get bad. Not dangerous, exactly, but bad in that particular city way, when a man does not strike you but carefully places you where, in his opinion, you belong.
"What 'that one'?"
"The one they locked up recently for insulting the watch. The wonder-man. Threatened everyone with great names, shouted, then lived with an orc and, so they say, became very well-mannered."
The square listened.

Anar saw it from the corner of his eye. The merchant with the wraps stopped counting coins. The woman with the blades lingered beside a stall. The half-orc with the chain hammer turned openly, waiting for more. Even the brazier by the wall seemed to crackle more quietly.
"They locked me up illegally," Anar said.
"Of course," said the guard. "Everyone in Agdash sits illegally. Especially the ones who scream at the watch."
"I am asking how to register for the tournament."
"And I am answering: you don't. Get out of here. I won't help you."

Anar looked at the guard's hand lying on the table. A broad palm. Rough fingers. Black dirt beneath the nails. An ordinary hand belonging to an ordinary city servant who had grown too used to deciding who was allowed where.
Something clicked softly in his head.

It was not an explosion. An explosion would have been easier. It was a cold, clear shift. The world narrowed to the guard's palm, to the mocking eyes, to the notice on the wall, to the memory of bars. The voices around him became muffled. The heat of Agdash retreated. Only the blue cold in his veins remained.
Mana rose inside him obediently, gladly, like a beast long kept on a chain.

First a spark appeared between his thumb and forefinger. Small, almost innocent. Then a second. A third. They ran over his knuckles, joined in thin lines, hissed. The air around Anar's hands trembled and filled with the sharp smell of ozone. Dust stirred on the nearest edge of the table.
Laren the scribe went pale.
The guard was no longer smiling.
"Put your hands down," he said.
"Write my name," Anar said.
"Put. Your hands. Down."
The guard's blade slid a finger's width from its sheath.
And then a stranger's hand settled on Anar's shoulder.
Not heavy. Not rough. Almost weightless.
But the mana in Anar's hands suddenly swayed as if the current had struck an invisible wall.
"Not here," said a voice behind him.
The voice was quiet. Dry. Without threat.
That was precisely why it was unsettling.
Anar froze. Blue discharges still crawled over his fingers, but weaker now. He slowly turned his head.

Behind him stood a man - or at least a being of human height and human outline. His body was hidden beneath layers of black cloth: dense, faded, frayed in places, yet arranged so that not a single edge hindered movement. His face was covered up to the eyes. His head was wrapped in dark bands beneath which neither hair nor ears could be seen. A long ragged cloak hung from his shoulders, like a scrap of night that had survived a fire. At his belt, the hilt of a curved blade could be guessed.
But the eyes were the main thing.
Beneath the shadow of the wrappings, they glowed with dull gold.
Not brightly, not like torches. More like coals under ash. Like something old, hidden, but not extinguished.

Anar did not dismiss the lightning immediately. First he wanted to ask who this was and why he was touching his shoulder. Then, for some reason, he changed his mind. There was no theatrical power in this stranger. He did not press. He did not hiss. He did not show off. He simply stood nearby, and the square around him became more careful.
The guard felt it too.
"Who are you?" he asked, but the arrogance had thinned.
The stranger did not answer him. He looked only at Anar.
"Come with me."
"Why would I?"

"Because if you hit a guard, they will imprison you again. If he hits you, you will answer. If you answer, someone will die. If someone dies at the western table of the arena, they will not release you after fifteen days."
Anar was silent for a moment.
The argument was annoyingly well built.
"He started it," he said.
"Cells rarely care."
Somewhere to the side, the half-orc gave a quiet snort.
Anar looked at the guard. The man clenched his jaw but said nothing. Apparently he too had decided that arguing with a golden-eyed unknown was not part of today's duty plan.
The blue sparks finally went out.
"Fine," Anar said. "But I still want to register."
"You will," said the stranger. "If you still want to after we speak."
He turned and walked away.
Anar stood for a second, feeling the whole square looking at him. Then he pointed two fingers at his own eyes and then toward the guard - a gesture universal even without translation - and followed.
Someone behind him laughed nervously.
The guard said nothing.

The stranger walked quickly, but without haste. He moved the way people move when they know where every stone has an edge, where every step is cracked, and where a space will open in the crowd a heartbeat before it opens. Anar had to speed up. This annoyed him. Especially because the stranger did not appear to speed up at all.

They passed the stalls near the arena, went beneath a side gallery, turned into a narrow passage between warehouses where it smelled of old leather and mice, then descended a stairway so steep any normal architect would have lost his license for it. Below, the world was quieter. The noise of the square remained above, blurred by stone. Here stood abandoned arched storehouses filled with broken shields, training dummies, rotten ropes, and sand that had probably once been carried out of the arena.
"Listen," Anar said when the silence grew too long. "Who are you?"
"Someone who dislikes stupid deaths."
"Very informative."
"Enough for me."
"Not enough for me."

The stranger stopped at a low wall, beyond which an old training ground opened up. A stone ring, half-covered in dust. Along its edges stood iron weapon racks, most of them empty. Several dummies leaned crookedly, like executed men whom someone had forgotten to let fall. In the center of the ground was a blackened patch of old fire.
The stranger vaulted lightly over the wall.
Anar climbed over after him with less grace.
"You want to enter the tournament," said the stranger.
"Yes."
"Why?"
Anar had expected any question except that one.
"What do you mean?"
"Why do you need the tournament?"
"To win."
"Why win?"
"Because it's a tournament. That's usually what people enter them for."
The stranger silently watched him.
Golden eyes beneath black cloth did not blink. Or blinked so rarely that it was worse.
Anar sighed.

"Money. Weapons. Status. So people stop thinking I'm some vagrant from another world. So I get on the fighter lists, get access somewhere that decides things more serious than who punched whom in an alley."
"And to prove the guard wrong."
"That's a bonus."
"A poor bonus. Pride kills faster than poison."
"In this world, everything kills faster than poison."
The stranger tilted his head slightly. Perhaps it was a smile, but the cloth hid too much.
"You said Avotu acknowledged your strength."
Anar grew wary.
"I did."
"Is it true?"
"Yes."
"Avotu rarely acknowledges strength aloud."
"Not exactly aloud. Well... he taught me. And saw what I could do. I throw lightning. Move fast. Once I even surprised him."
"A master is easy to surprise if you do something foolish with confidence."
"Thanks. Very supportive."
"I am not supporting you. I am checking."
Anar narrowed his eyes.
"Checking what?"
"Whether you are worth my time."

The phrase struck precisely where Anar had developed a bruise over the past few days. Not on his face - deeper. In the place where Zhenya's busy look had landed, and Yura's brief conversation, and Ravan's teasing, and Alexander's palace distance, and his own feeling of uselessness.
"And who said I need your time?"
The stranger raised a hand and pointed to the training ground.
"You did."
"I didn't say that."
"You nearly attacked a city guard because of registration for a tournament where you will most likely die. That is a long way of saying: help me."
Anar wanted to answer sharply. He even opened his mouth.
But the words stuck.
Because it hurt not because it was rude. It hurt because it was accurate.

The stranger took the cloak from his shoulders and tossed it onto the low wall. Beneath it were the same dark layers of cloth, wrapped tightly around his body. No heavy armor. No pauldrons, spikes, gleaming plates. Only belts, soft leather bracers, and the hilt of a curved blade at his hip.
"A short duel," he said.
"Right now?"
"You wanted the arena."
"I wanted to register, not fight the first black curtain I met."
"In the arena, the first one you meet will not ask whether you are ready."
Anar looked at the empty racks.
"Weapons?"
"You have none."
"I have lightning."
"Then you have a weapon."
"And you?"
The stranger touched the hilt of his blade but did not draw it.
"I will manage."
"Now that sounds insulting."
"Good."

The curved blade came out of its sheath without a sound. The metal was dark, matte, with a thin pale line along the cutting edge. It bore no ornament except barely visible notches near the base. The weapon did not look ceremonial. It looked personal. Like a thing cleaned of blood many times and never once called beautiful.
The stranger reversed the blade and held it lightly, point down.
"Begin."
Anar did not argue.
He struck at once.

Not with full force. After all, he did not want to kill the unclear type who had possibly just saved him from prison. But sharply enough to show that yes, he was not a boy with a wooden sword in a courtyard.
Blue lightning tore from his fingers and lashed across the ground.
The stranger was there.
And then he was not.
The discharge hit a dummy by the wall. It flared, jerked, and collapsed into two smoking halves.
Anar blinked.
The stranger's blade lay flat against his shoulder.
"Dead."
Anar jerked away, turning at the same time. An unpleasant pinch went through his chest. Not fear. Surprise.
"I wasn't ready."
"In the arena, those are usually the last words."
"Again."
"Go on."

This time Anar did not attack immediately. He stepped aside, raised his hands, let thin discharges run over his fingers. Avotu had once said: do not drag mana, guide it. A river does not like being pulled by the hair. Anar tried to remember that feeling. The current through shoulders, elbows, wrists. Not force. A path.
The stranger stood still.
That was more irritating than movement.
Anar lunged.
His body blurred into a blue trace. Stone dust exploded beneath his feet. He appeared at the stranger's side and struck at the ribs with his palm, releasing a short electric pulse.
His palm hit emptiness.

Black cloth flashed before his eyes, and something struck his wrist. Not an edge - the hilt or the flat of the blade. His fingers went numb. The lightning tore into the ground, leaving a thin glowing crack in the stone.
The next blow came under his knee.
Anar dropped to one knee and barely managed to roll when the blade passed through the place where his neck had been a moment before.
"Dead," said the stranger.
"You like that word?"
"It is useful."

Anar sprang up. His cheeks burned. The training ground no longer seemed empty. Every stone, every rack, every shadow had suddenly become part of the fight, and all of them were on the stranger's side.
The third exchange lasted longer.

Anar began working in series. Short discharges, step, slip, feint, burst. He did not know the proper names, did not know the stance, did not know how it was "supposed" to be done. But his body remembered speed, and mana obeyed better than before. The ten days in the cell, spent with a little spark moving between his fingers, had not been wasted. Now he could do more than explode the air. He could hold the current thin, sharp, controlled.
Once, the stranger truly stepped back.
Only half a step.
But Anar saw it.
And felt a flash of wicked joy.
"Aha," he breathed.
"Do not celebrate during a fight."
Black cloth swept upward.

Anar took an open-palmed strike to the chest. It did not look powerful, but all the air left his lungs at once, as if someone had pulled out a stopper. He flew backward, slid on his back across the dusty stone, and stopped beside the broken stump of a rack.
The sky above the ground was a narrow strip between the warehouse roofs. Gray, hot, foreign.
Anar lay there and tried to breathe.
The stranger approached. His blade was already sheathed.
"Dead," he said for the third time.
"I got it," Anar rasped.
"No, you didn't."
"Great. Explain, since you're so smart."
The stranger crouched beside him. His golden eyes were calm. Without mockery. That was almost worse.
"You have a great deal of power. Too much for someone who does not know where to place his left foot."
Anar slowly sat up, holding his chest.
"My left foot is offended."

"You are fast, but you enter in a straight line. You hit hard, but you announce it first with every muscle in your face. You hold mana in your hands as if it were a torch, not blood. You get angry before attacking. You breathe badly. You look at the weapon instead of the shoulders. After a successful move, you rejoice. After a failed one, you take offense. And every time words touch you, you stop being a fighter and become a boy whose pride has been stepped on."
Anar said nothing.
It was a long list. The worst part was that almost all of it sounded true.
"But the lightning is pretty," he said at last.
The stranger bowed his head slightly.
"Pretty things often die first."
"Are you always this cheerful?"
"No. Today I am gentle."
Anar snorted despite himself. The laugh hurt because his chest still ached.
The stranger stood and offered him a hand.
Anar looked at it.
The hand wore a dark fingerless glove. Old scars marked the knuckles. Not decorative scars. Not heroic scars. Just traces of other people's teeth, stone, iron, and time.
Anar accepted the help and rose.

At that moment, had any of the old arena men seen the black figure on the abandoned ground, had they noticed the movement of his shoulders, the way he held the blade, the habit of never leaving open space behind his back, they might have remembered a name that in Agdash had been spoken more and more softly for five years.
Utmysh.

Six times he had entered the Ring on the days of great tournaments. Six times he had left victorious. Not the strongest, not the tallest, not the brightest. Simply the last one standing. They had called him the Black Mask, the Sand Shadow, the Silent Blade. Then, after his sixth victory, he disappeared. Some said the northern houses had bought him. Others said he had died beyond the walls. Still others said King Agsham himself had given him a secret task. Agdash loved rumors because rumors were cheaper than food.
Almost no one knew the truth.
Anar, of course, knew nothing.
To him, the man before him was simply a strange type in black who had killed him three times in five minutes and now looked as if that had only been a greeting.
"Well?" Anar asked. "Did you check?"
"Yes."
"And?"
"Avotu was not wrong."
Anar unexpectedly stopped being angry.
The phrase was short. Dry. But for some reason it landed deeper than all the guard's mockery.
"So I can enter?"
"You can."
"Excellent."
"And you will die."
"Why ruin it immediately?"
"Because between 'can' and 'ready' lies work. You are not ready."
Anar brushed dust from his sleeve. His fingers still trembled slightly after the discharges.
"How long until the tournament?"
"Seven days."
"Can someone prepare in seven days?"
"For victory? No."
"For what, then?"
"To survive the first fight. Possibly the second. If you start listening."
Anar looked at him more carefully.
"Are you offering to train me?"
"Yes."
"Why?"

The stranger turned toward the edge of the ground. Somewhere above, the arena's noise came again: a merchant's shout, a hammer blow, the whinny of some animal, laughter. Agdash lived. Pressed. Chewed anyone who got between its teeth.
"Because power without form is a fire inside your own house," he said. "And right now you are burning from within and calling it character."
"You speak beautifully."
"I was silent for a long time. It built up."
"And what, every day?"
"Until the tournament - every day. Dawn. Here. No lateness."
"And if I don't come?"
"Then the guard was right."
Anar sharply raised his eyes.

The stranger had already drawn the cloak back around himself. Black cloth covered his shoulders, his face, the hilt of his blade. Once again he became a piece of shadow, the kind the city cast even at noon for some reason.
"That's manipulation," Anar said.
"Does it work?"
Anar grimaced.
"Unfortunately."
"Then until dawn."
The stranger headed for the exit from the training ground.
"Hey," Anar called.
He stopped but did not turn around.
"What's your name?"
The silence lasted a little longer than it should have.
"Call me Mask."
"Seriously?"
"No. But it will be enough for you."
"And how do I register?"
"Come to the western table tomorrow after training. Tell Laren the Black Mask ordered him to put your name on the list."
"And he'll believe me?"
"He will."
"And the guard?"
"The guard will pretend he did not hear."
Anar smiled crookedly.
"I'm already starting to like this plan."
The stranger finally turned his head. In the narrow slit between the layers of cloth, golden eyes gleamed again.
"Do not confuse a plan with hope."
"What's the difference?"
"A plan requires you to rise before dawn tomorrow."
With that, he left.
Anar remained alone on the training ground.

Dust settled slowly. In the burned dummy by the wall, a blue spark still smoldered, stubbornly refusing to go out. Somewhere in a crack between stones crawled a tiny gray beetle, utterly indifferent to tournaments, legends, Sivarus, Avotu, pride, and human attempts to find meaning in a world that should have fallen apart long ago.
Anar walked to the dummy and nudged it with the toe of his boot.
The charred upper half fell away.
"Dead," Anar said in the stranger's dry tone.
Then he winced.
"Annoying."

He raised his hands. A small blue spark appeared between his fingers. Not angry. Not explosive. Quiet, even, as it had been in the cell on the tenth day. Anar watched it crawl from index finger to middle finger, then to ring finger, then back again. He remembered the left foot. Set it slightly differently. Stupidly, awkwardly, but differently.
Somewhere above, the city kept making noise.
Agdash still did not like him.
But for the first time in a long while, Anar felt that he had a place he needed to be in the morning.
It was little.
But in a dying world, little sometimes became the beginning of everything.
